Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:35: And the end of his words there teaches you that no good comes out of wine. And especially students of Torah must be careful of excessive wine, and that wine brings on sleep - and our Sages, of blessed memory, said in Sanhedrin (chapter 8, mishnah 5), "wine and sleep for the wicked - good for them and good for the world; for the righteous - bad for them and bad for the world" - for wine is harmful for the righteous, because it increases sleep and they come to be idle from the words of Torah. And this is why King Solomon, peace be upon him, after condemning wine, praised wisdom, saying (Proverbs 24:1), "do not envy evil men, nor desire to be with them," and so on, and afterward said (24:3), "through wisdom a house is built," and said (24:5), "a wise man is strong, and a man of knowledge increases strength," and afterward said (24:10), "if you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small" - and they said, of blessed memory, in Midrash Mishlei on this verse, Rabbi Abahu said, whoever weakens himself from the words of Torah has no strength to stand in the day of adversity - and in the Zohar, Parashat Vayetze (page 152b), they elaborate in explaining this verse, and we shall copy it in its place. It follows that wine is, for a Torah scholar, a cause for him to grow weak in the words of Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:36: And you shall find that they said in the Mishnah (Ta'anit, chapter 2, mishnah 7), the men of the priestly watch are permitted to drink wine at night but not by day, while the men of the ancestral house [officiating that day] are forbidden neither by day nor by night. And Rashi explains: "at night," there is no concern that the service might become too heavy, for they saw already in the evening that the offerings had ceased and the service was not heavy. "Not by day," for many offerings might come and the men of the ancestral house would not suffice for that whole day, and these [the watch] would need to assist them, and they would be unfit for service because of drunkenness. "The men of the ancestral house, neither by day nor by night," because they would spend the whole night bringing up limbs and fats that had fallen off the altar, or, if they had not finished by day, they would finish at night - but the men of the watch do not need to assist at night in turning with the fork, for the ancestral house can suffice alone for turning the arrangement [of wood] - to this point. We find, then, that we learn that whoever's service was heavy upon them was forbidden wine, so that they not come to be idle from the service. And so whoever wishes to bear the yoke of Torah and not come to be idle from it should distance himself from wine.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:37: And they said in the Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar, Parashat Vayera, beginning of page 110), in these words: Rabbi Yitzchak said, the evil inclination is never enticed except through eating and drinking, and through the joy of wine it then rules over a person. Concerning the righteous, what is written of him? (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul," and he never becomes drunk - for Rabbi Yehudah said, this young Torah scholar who becomes drunk, I apply to him (ibid. 11:22), "a gold ring in a pig's snout," and not only that, but he desecrates the Name of Heaven. What is the practice of the wicked? "Behold joy and gladness" (Isaiah 22:13) - wine then rules over a person - "slaying oxen and killing sheep," and so on (Isaiah, ibid.) - and concerning them Scripture says (Isaiah 5:11), "woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink" - in order to arouse the evil inclination, for the evil inclination is aroused only through wine, as it is said (Genesis 19:33), "and they made their father drink wine" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:38: And concerning the intent of eating and drinking, by the plain meaning, Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor that one should be happy with his portion, and trust in his Maker that He will provide his sustenance, and not restrict himself with the exactitudes of poverty. And so they said in the Midrash, "all the days of the poor are evil" - meaning, whoever is poor in his faith and grows weary of expense, and if he acquires livelihood for himself, fears that he will decline in his possessions and need people - he is found in sorrow and worry all his days; but whoever is happy with his portion and believes in the Holy One, blessed be He, that He shall provide his sustenance whenever he needs it, his heart is always joyful and of good cheer, as though a table were set and a feast were always before him. And further we read in the Midrash, "better a dry morsel with quiet than [a house full of feasting with strife]" (Proverbs 17:1) - this is one who is happy with his portion, and shall always be at ease and tranquil, since he is happy with what the Holy One, blessed be He, provided him; he shall never steal or rob, and is found calm and confident all his days. "Than a house full of sacrifices with strife" - this is one who is not happy with his portion, but pursues coarse foods, and steals and robs to satisfy his desire, and is found all his days in strife and quarrel and pursued by people. And one who eats little to satisfy his soul and does not intend his own bodily benefit recognizes his Creator - for when he hungers he shall understand his own lack and the lowliness of man, that at the time he lacks a portion of bread and a jug of water, his strength and all his limbs weaken, his eyes darken, and he lacks the strength to stand on his feet - and then he shall recognize the perfection of the Holy One, blessed be He, who needs neither eating nor drinking, as it is said (Psalms 50:13), "shall I eat the flesh of bulls," and so on. And when he hungers he shall lift his eyes to the Holy One, blessed be He, to seek his sustenance, and know that He, blessed be His Name, gives bread to all flesh, and provides sustenance for each and every one, and for every single body enough for its lack. And then he shall have mercy on the poor and separate from pride, since coarse foods bring a person to sins and guilt, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked," and it is written (ibid. 11:15), "and you shall eat and be satisfied - take heed to yourselves," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:39: And what is praiseworthy in a person concerning eating is three things: the first, that he content himself with his portion, even a little, and not seek more; second, that he eat at its proper time, before he becomes very hungry and his limbs weaken and he comes to illness, and has no strength to serve the Holy One, blessed be He, properly, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:16), "and your princes eat in the morning"; third, that he not intend in his eating his bodily pleasure but only the sustenance of his soul, and not follow his desire to eat everything his palate craves, evil foods, because they are harmful. And Ramban, of blessed memory, wrote that a person should always eat less than a third [of what would satisfy him]. And they said, of blessed memory (Gittin 70a), a meal from which you derive pleasure, withdraw your hand from it - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:40: And the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot, of blessed memory (Gate of Abstinence, chapter 5), wrote concerning abstinence in eating, in these words: and it is fitting for you, my brother, to conduct yourself with abstinence from the permitted pleasures within your ability, until they appear in your eyes like the nature of pleasures forbidden to you - meaning, like [forbidden] fat and the like - lest you abandon your Torah and neglect your duty. And you have already noted what the blessed Creator commanded the king, saying (Deuteronomy 17:17), "he shall not multiply wives for himself," and saying (ibid. 17:16), "only he shall not multiply horses for himself," and saying (cf. Nehemiah 13:26), "did not Solomon king of Israel sin because of these?" - despite all the strength of his intellect and the abundance of his understanding and greatness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:41: And he says further there, and strive to restrict the sense of taste, so that you take from food and drink only enough for your sustenance, and abstain from what is more than this. And the strategy for this matter is that you minimize the kinds of relish, and rely on one relish while you can, and likewise accustom your soul, at certain times, to be without relish, in order to train your belly and your nature, until the matter becomes easy for you when you refrain from it. And if you can forgo relish that involves labor and toil, and rely on what involves no labor at all, such as olives, figs, grapes, and the like, do so - and make your daytime eating lighter than your nighttime eating, if it is your custom to eat several times during the day, so that the movement of your limbs be light by day and the matters of your Torah and your worldly affairs be easy for you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:42: And afterward you shall practice fasting your body, if your body is strong, even one day a week, and everything you can accustom your soul to, not to feel concerning eating and drinking, in order to discipline it, do it, and make your intent in it more for healing than for nourishment - and let all your drinking be water, unless your intent with wine is to drink for the benefit of your body or to remove worry from your heart, as it is said (Proverbs 31:6), "give strong drink to the one who is perishing" - and be careful about excess of it and indulgence in it, and the gathering of people over it, for it is the great affliction for Torah and for the world - and the sage has already told of it what suffices (Proverbs 20:1), "wine is a scoffer, strong drink a brawler," and he says concerning food and drink (ibid. 23:20), "be not among winebibbers," and so on, "for the glutton and the drunkard shall come to poverty," and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:43: And this way the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote is the way of abstinence fitting for masters of Torah, whose main craft is Torah - for if a master of Torah wishes to rely on trust and spend his money eating meat or chickens and the like, kinds of pleasures, he is found troubling himself with the affairs of this world in pursuit of sustenance, and shall be idle from the words of Torah - and at a time he cannot find his custom, he shall not be able to bear it and shall fall ill. Therefore it is fitting for every Torah scholar to practice this abstinence that is written in Chovot HaLevavot.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:44: And so there are several teachings of our Rabbis that support this and distance pleasures from masters of Torah - among them, first, the Baraita of "the acquisition of Torah" (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 4-5): this is the way of Torah - you shall eat bread with salt, and so on - do not crave the table of kings. And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, asked only for "bread to eat and clothing to wear" (Genesis 28:20) - and through this the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, are fulfilled, who said (Parashat Terumah, page 141a), happy is he who derives no pleasure at all from its own [the husk]. And especially if he eats only for healing, as the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote, this is the more excellent aspect, that he derives no benefit at all from its own.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:45: And so it is fitting for whoever wishes to sanctify himself that he eat only for healing, so that he not fall ill and be idle from Torah and commandments - therefore it is fitting that he not fill his soul with coarse foods, and even from good things he should not fully satisfy his desire, even on the Sabbath, for much eating causes much sleep, as they said, of blessed memory, in the first chapter of Yoma (mishnah, chapter 8 - actually referring to the High Priest before Yom Kippur), they would not feed him much, for food brings on sleep. And when he trains himself to content himself with a little, he shall find rest for his soul, and be sanctified in Torah, and shall not come to belch while studying.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:46: And the wise person shall take this matter to heart, and abstain from his desire, and not fill his belly and his desire like a beast, for "who is mighty? He who subdues his inclination" (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 1) - and if his inclination entices him to eat, he shall break his strength and subdue it from his desire, and then fear and holiness shall rest upon him, as it is written (Psalms 34:10), "fear the LORD, His holy ones."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:47: And so the Ra'avad wrote in the Gate of Holiness, in these words: and I see that the great fence, the excellent guard, and the good path for subduing the inclination, is the hunger of the soul from minimizing its pleasures and delights in food and drink - except that he may enjoy a good aroma, and washing in hot water, since hot water is pleasant to him, and the little food he eats should be well seasoned and prepared, since it is pleasant to him, and his soul shall accept it and be content with a little of it - and he should always leave a little short of his full need and the completion of his desire, and shall not drink wine except well diluted, so that his mind not be confused by it. And along this path they said, of blessed memory (Gittin 70a), a meal from which you derive pleasure, withdraw your hand from it - and there are two great benefits in this matter: the first, that its eating not harm him, and the second, the subduing of the inclination and the breaking of desire. And just as we have said concerning a meal, so is the way for all the world's pleasures and delights, that a person not fill his full desire from them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:48: And needless to say that a person should guard himself from foods he knows to be harmful to him, for one who eats things harmful to him when he could avoid them is negligent of his body and negligent of his soul, because he follows his desire and does not care about the loss of his body - and this is the way of the evil inclination and its foolish counsel, to entice him from the way of life to the way of death. And every living, speaking being knows that the evil inclination has no way to him except through the way of the permitted, and the opening of its path is from what is permitted to him - and if he guards the opening, he needs no other guard.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:49: And I have already set forth everything before you at the beginning of this Gate, that the way of that worthless counselor is to advise him to fill his desire from what is permitted to him, and after habituating him to filling his desire with what is permitted, and inducing his soul to be constantly eager and yearning for its pledge, it entices him toward the light prohibition, and from the light to the severe, as I have said. Therefore be careful with the permitted, and if you fence yourself with it and minimize your desire from what is permitted to you, you are assured that your inclination will no longer entice you toward the forbidden - for if a matter of prohibition arises, you immediately reason this a fortiori argument within yourself: if I was forbidden in what is permitted to me, how much more so in what is forbidden to me? And since you carry this a fortiori argument upon yourself, you are assured that you shall abstain from the lustful thought, and all the more so from the deed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:50: And a person should not afflict his soul [excessively], lest he weaken his heart and his deeds and his nature become corrupted, and his mind become confused, and his loss be greater than his gain, for he shall be idle from Torah and from prayer, and if he studies, his Torah shall not be settled, and he shall not agree properly on halachah and the dialectics of tradition, since Torah is acquired only through the essence of joy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:51: And a person should not withhold himself from any joy of a commandment or any pleasure of a commandment, only let his eyes be open against the inclination, and be careful that it not fill all his desires. And if he weakens his heart from eating too little, it is better for him to eat twice a day, little by little, and not fill his belly all at once - and if it is not convenient for him to eat twice a day, let him have among the confections that settle the heart, and eat a little of them, and his heart shall be strengthened. Also, if he sees in himself and by nature that he needs to fast a day or two, let him fast according to his condition, for one who sits in fasting when he needs it is called holy, provided he not be idle from Torah or from commandments because of it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:52: Also, the oath, which is severe, was permitted to fence oneself at a time of transgression, as Boaz said concerning Ruth (Ruth 3:13), "as the LORD lives, lie down until morning" - our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Vayikra Rabbah 23:11), that his inclination accused him all night, saying to him, you are unmarried and she is unmarried, and a woman is acquired through intercourse - go and have relations with her and she shall be acquired to you through intercourse. Boaz leaped up and swore against the inclination, "as the LORD lives, lie down until morning" - he swore to the inclination that he would not do this, and to the woman, lie down until morning. So every person can know for himself the fence that would be good for him, whether subduing [his desire] or an oath. And I see that nothing is better than subduing and hunger of the soul, as I have said - and if he needs an oath as well, let him swear and fulfill it, along the lines of what David said (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to observe Your righteous judgments" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:53: And I, the youngest, say that this way is good for whoever it is possible for and has the means to acquire confections, but whoever is poor and lacks the means to conduct himself this way should at least conduct his eating according to what is needed for health, as Rambam wrote in Hilchot De'ot (chapter 4), in what he wrote, that a person should minimize his eating, for this is the correct way. Especially one who does not fast - it is good that he minimize his morning meal so that he not be idle from the occupation with Torah, and he should gauge in his mind that his measure of eating be in two sessions, morning and evening, equal to the measure of what he was accustomed to being satisfied by at one time.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:54: And for whoever wishes to be constant in rising at midnight to occupy himself with Torah, let him put his main eating in the morning meal, and at night eat only fruits - and let them be dried fruits, such as raisins, almonds, walnuts, and figs. And let him distance himself at night from eating coarse foods, such as cheese and the like, but rather conduct himself as the Ra'avad wrote above, at the beginning of his words, that he eat a little, well seasoned and prepared, and the bread be less than the cooked dish - and for whoever wishes to read most of the night, it is good that he not eat bread at all at night. And so my teacher, peace be upon him, was accustomed, when he was not fasting. And a penitent accustomed to fasting every day, on days when he shall eat, such as Rosh Chodesh and festivals, should conduct himself along this way we have written.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:55: And for whoever the way the Ra'avad, peace be upon him, wrote is possible, as a repair for the day, it is good as a repair for the night, that he eat at night only kinds of confections that settle the heart - and through this he can withstand most of the night in the occupation with Torah without sleep - and it is found that through this he bears some affliction, and does not pursue pleasures, for Torah endures only in one who distances himself from pleasure, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, page 247a), on the verse (cf. Numbers 28:5), "fine flour mixed with beaten oil" - it is explained there that "fine flour" is the Shechinah; "mixed with oil," it says of it, this is the oil that flows and goes forth from above. And it says afterward, the Ra'aya Meheimna said, holy lamp, how sweet are your words - certainly it is said here, "mixed with beaten oil," and it is said there concerning the Oral Torah, "mixed" with Scripture, with Mishnah, and with Talmud, and so on. And there is a second secret: "mixed with beaten oil" - certainly Torah is not "mixed" except for one who endures several poundings for its sake, as the masters of the Mishnah established, that Torah endures only in one who kills himself over it. And it says further, at the time you pound your feet from country to country, you shall merit to see the countenance of the Shechinah. And further, "mixed with beaten oil" - this is one who fulfills "you shall eat bread with salt, and drink water by measure." And further, "mixed with beaten oil" - this is what is written (Isaiah 53:5), "and he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:56: Behold, it is explicit that the Torah, called "fine flour," endures in a person only if he pounds himself and kills himself and fulfills "you shall eat bread with salt." And although it says "and further" [several times], all these explanations come to one place - that the intent is the pounding of matter so that the Torah and the soul shine within it, and this is the way to attain Torah - that even if he is wealthy, he should not practice indulgences for himself - and this is what it says (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 4), "this is the way of Torah," and so on. And this is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 119:71), "it is good for me that I was afflicted, so that I might learn Your statutes."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:57: And it says in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, page 11a) that Rashbi, peace be upon him, and Rabbi Elazar, when they came out of the cave, and Rabbi Pinchas went to see him - they said, of blessed memory: he went to him and found him with a changed appearance, his body full of cracks [sores]. He wept with him and said, woe, that I see you thus. He said, happy is my portion that you see me thus, for had you not seen me thus, I would not be thus - to this point. And so they said in the Talmud, Tractate Shabbat (33b). Behold, it is explicit that through the sufferings he endured in the cave, he attained wondrous wisdom - and so they said in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, that in the thirteen years Rashbi, peace be upon him, was confined in the cave, the depths of wisdom were revealed to him and he attained knowledge of future things.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:58: And especially one who has sins must endure sufferings for his sins and shall not merit the supernal light, which is the oil concerning which David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 23:5), "You anoint my head with oil" - unless he pounds himself. And this is what it says, "and further, 'mixed with beaten oil' - this is what is written, 'and he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities'" - and the intent is that just as the Messiah suffers, our iniquities cause him to be crushed - if so, whoever wishes that the Messiah not be crushed by our iniquities should himself suffer and be crushed. And so it is explained in Sefer Chasidim (siman 528), that a certain pious man endured several sufferings for his sins and gave this reason mentioned - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:59: Further, in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, brought in the Yalkut, Parashat Va'etchanan (siman 830, page 265, col. 3), on the verse "I am the LORD your God," in these words: a person who does not merit that the Torah enter into his bowels should seek mercy concerning excessive eating and drinking, that it not enter his bowels, as it is said (Isaiah 48:10), "I have refined you, but not with silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction" - just as this furnace, even if you put into it all the wood in the world, burns and destroys it, so a person's throat, even if you give it all the foods in the world, destroys them - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:60: Further, they said in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 19:1): Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said, words of Torah require blackening and evening [dedication morning and evening] - and where do we know of sustenance? "Who provides for the raven its prey" (Job 38:41) - so, unless a person becomes cruel toward his own body, his children, and his household, like this raven, he does not merit the words of Torah - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:61: And the reason the Torah does not rest upon a person except after he distances pleasures from himself is because the Torah is called holy, as it is said (Proverbs 2:5), "and you shall find the knowledge of God" - and therefore it rests only in a place where there is holiness and abstinence from bodily pleasures.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:62: And Rabbi Yisrael, of blessed memory, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor: great is the Torah, whose holiness is such that even from bread and water Moses needed to sanctify himself before receiving the Torah, as it is said (Exodus 34:28), "and he was there with the LORD" [forty days and forty nights, without bread or water] - and is this not an a fortiori argument? If from bread and water, which are pure, he needed to sanctify himself for forty days, how much more so should we sanctify ourselves for the words of Torah from all impurity - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:63: And what appears to me concerning the intent of eating, according to what is understood from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, is what is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 154b), that there is a supernal table upon which is the showbread - and it says, and from the secret of this table, sustenance goes out to the world, according to what is given into it from above, and that bread is the fruit and sustenance that goes out from this table, to show that from this table fruits, produce, and sustenance go out to the world - if there were no vineyard, the grapes that are its fruit, going out from it, would not be found; if there were no tree, its fruit would not be found in the world - therefore the table is the essential thing, and the sustenance that goes out from it is that bread.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:64: And it says further there, a person's table must be found in cleanliness of the body, that he not come close to eat his food except in cleanliness of himself - and therefore a person must first empty himself, before he eats the sustenance of a clean table - for that sustenance he prepares for himself, in which the Holy One, blessed be He, delights, is so that vomit and excrement, which are from the secret of the Other Side, not come near that table, and the Other Side receives nothing at all from the sustenance of this table. Afterward, once a person has eaten and delighted, he must give a portion of the residue to that side - and what is it? The "final waters" [washing after the meal] - that filth of the hands that must be given to that side, the portion it needs - and this is certainly a debt, and it rests where the debt rests, and it is an obligation upon a person to give it this portion - and therefore no blessing at all is needed [for it], since blessing does not belong to that side. And therefore a person must not give the food from his table to that vomit and excrement, and all the more so within his own intestines, and all the more so since it is good for a person and for the health and repair of his body - and therefore the table is for eating from it in cleanliness, as has been said - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:65: Now, with the reason stated in this teaching, that it is forbidden to give a portion of one's food to that vomit and excrement, we shall also understand the reason for (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - the reason being that since this food is alluded to as coming from the supernal table, it is not fitting that the external force have a portion in it, being what is called vomit and excrement - and just as it happens physically, so it happens spiritually: from the supernal food, the soul certainly derives benefit, and therefore it is not fitting that the husk derive benefit there from the food itself, which is holy - and so that it not accuse us concerning this, we give it its portion in the "final waters."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:66: And with this is the end of the teaching, which returns to say, "and therefore a person must not give the food from his table to that vomit and excrement, and all the more so within his intestines" - for this was already said at greater length above, that he must empty himself. And further, what does it mean "and all the more so within his intestines"? Is this not obviously what we are discussing?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:67: Rather, the matter is that the food a person eats at his table indicates a supernal holiness upon him - for he first sanctifies his hands, as we shall explain in the repairs of the table, and afterward blesses the blessing "HaMotzi" over the bread - and the blessing over every fruit and over bread is to bestow upon it spirituality from the great Name YHVH, who brings everything into being, and who gives soul and existence to all created things, and who created this bread through all that is bound to the Name mentioned - for no created thing is created except through the Cause of all who brings everything into existence, as explained in the Tikkunim (page 116a), in these words: rather, just as there is no partner for the letter Vav from another letter, so it has no partner, for it is one and there is no second to it, one without number - it created everything and there is no creator over it - and can anyone create even a small gnat but it? Rather, waters have the power to create trees and grasses, and they are created - but the Creator of the worlds created, and there is none who created it - to this point. And through the blessing and the mention of the Name, we arouse the supernal flow upon that bread or that fruit, as at the beginning of its creation through the Name - it follows that his intent in eating is that the soul benefit from the spirituality of the great Name clothed in that fruit - it follows that there is in it a portion of life, in the secret of (Nehemiah 9:6), "and You give life to them all" - and likewise water, called "living water," is so in secret through the blessing we bless over it. And whoever eats his food in this manner is called a living righteous person, and cleaves to the supernal life, and refines his eating to give a portion to the soul. And we shall further elaborate below on this matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:68: And now there is in this good reason why it is not fitting to give of the holy food to the external force - and this is what it says above, "to empty himself, before he eats the sustenance of a clean table, for that sustenance he prepares for himself, in which the Holy One, blessed be He, delights." And these are two aspects: the first, concerning the food itself, which is holy; the second, concerning the table - and its saying "in which the Holy One, blessed be He, delights" teaches the matter mentioned. And corresponding to this it says two things, that one must give the residue and not the food - water, which he washes, which is filth, not from the essence of the food that is at the table. And it returns to say "and therefore," because a difficulty arose for it, that after all we find that in the offering they would give it a portion in the matter of limbs and fats, as explained in Parashat Terumah (page 141a), that the smoke would bend toward the north side - and so it would be fitting that at the table, called the altar, a portion of the food be given to it, and it would have been good not to empty oneself. And to this it answers, "and therefore a person must not give the food from his table to that vomit and excrement" - and its saying "from his table" teaches that his table is a table that is before the LORD, and it is not fitting to give from it to dogs, called vomit and excrement - behold, even the vomit and excrement are outside it. "And all the more so within his intestines" - for within him is holy, being the holy soul, a portion of Him, blessed be He, and it derives benefit from the food, and it is not fitting that the husk derive benefit there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:69: And the reason for the food of the soul is that, in truth, it would be better if it did not eat and could exist without eating at all - but the matter is, without doubt, that before its coming into this world it stands above and enjoys the radiance of the Shechinah, and the supernal beings, if they did not enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah, their existence would be nullified, for that illumination is the cause of their existence - and so it is explained in the Midrash of the Zohar (Parashat Balak, page 208a; Parashat Terumah, page 156b). And against its will, they bring it down and clothe it in a body - and now, because of the cause of separation from the supernal source, it is impossible for it to enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah because of the separating curtain of the body. And Israel in the wilderness enjoyed somewhat from the radiance of the Shechinah, namely the secret of the manna, which is supernal light made physical, as explained in the Zohar (ibid.) - and therefore it was absorbed into the limbs (Yoma 75b) and was food for the body and soul as one. However, afterward they ate from the produce of the land, meaning that the flow became physical and thickened in the supernal land and in this land - which was not so with the manna, which did not thicken in the supernal land, as it is written (Exodus 16:4), "behold, I shall rain down" - it was only passing through in a manner of transit; it did not thicken in it, and therefore it had a portion for man and a portion for the external force, namely the excess, vomit and excrement. If so, a person is compelled to eat in order to give a spiritual portion to his soul, that it be cleaving and enjoy somewhat from the radiance of the Shechinah, through the ways we have mentioned.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:70: And there is some support for this in the matter of the four foods that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, Parashat Beshalach, page 61b), in these words: he said that Israel, at the beginning of their exodus from Egypt, ate matzah, which is the attribute of righteousness [Tzedek]; afterward, when they circumcised and uncovered, they merited to eat the manna, bread from heaven. He says afterward, the colleagues who strive in Torah are nourished from another, supernal place - what is it? As it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "and wisdom gives life to those who have it" - a more supernal place. Rabbi Elazar said to him, if so, why is their soul weaker than the rest of the people of the world, when they should appear with greater power and strength? He said to him, your question is fitting - come and see, all the sustenance of the people of the world comes from above; that sustenance that comes from heaven and this earth is the sustenance of the whole world, and it is coarse and thick food; and that sustenance that comes from higher above is sustenance that comes through judgment, and from the place where judgment is found, it is a more refined sustenance - the sustenance found for Israel at that time, from the supernal place called "heaven," was a more refined sustenance, which enters the soul more than anything and is more separated from the body, and is called "wretched bread" [lechem hakelokel]. The sustenance more supernal than everything is the sustenance of the colleagues, those who strive in Torah, who eat the sustenance of ru'ach and neshamah, and do not eat the sustenance of the body at all - and this is from a place more supernal and precious than everything, called Chokhmah - therefore the body of the colleagues is weaker than that of the people of the world, for they do not eat the sustenance of the body at all, but eat the sustenance of ru'ach and neshamah, from a place distant and precious beyond everything, and therefore that sustenance is the most refined of the refined, of all - happy is their portion. This is what is written, "wisdom gives life to those who have it" - happy is the portion of the body that can be nourished with the food of the soul - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:71: And one should not explain what it says concerning Torah scholars, that they do not eat the food of the body at all, as meaning that they do not eat at all - for we find that they did eat. And it says further there (page 62b), Rabbi Yesa would not prepare his meal every day until he sought his request before the Holy One, blessed be He, saying, we shall not prepare the meal until it is given from the King's house - after seeking his request before the Holy One, blessed be He, he would wait one hour and say, now is the time it is given from the King's house - from here onward they would prepare the meal - and this is the way of those who fear the Holy One, blessed be He, and fear sin - to this point. And although it is explained in Parashat Shemot in the Zohar (page 15a) that Rashbi, peace be upon him, and his colleagues stood two days without eating because they were occupied with Torah, not knowing whether it was day or night, nevertheless certainly afterward they ate. And it would be fitting, since the Torah is their food, that they not be sustained by physical food - if so, we must understand what it means that they do not eat the food of the body at all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:72: However, the plain sense of the matter is this: the food - meaning, the supernal flow - is bestowed within this physical food a person eats, according to the level of the person's soul - and even though the sage and the ignorant person eat the same measure of bread, or the measure of one meal, each one is flowed his food from the level of his soul, from the place he holds fast to, and along these lines it shall be thick and coarse, or fine. And this is what it says, "the body of the colleagues is weaker than that of the people of the world, for they do not eat the food of the body at all" - and the intent is that even though they eat the measure of a meal like the rest of the people eat, the body shall be weak, because the spiritual flow bestowed in that food is fine, and it is entirely the food of the soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:73: And one should not explain that this is because most Torah scholars are poor and their eating is scant, and that scant amount is the eating of the soul, along the lines of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, for whom a kav of carobs sufficed from Sabbath to Sabbath (Berachot 17b) - for it says "colleagues" without qualification. And so it says further there, concerning the division of the four foods (page 62a), that it says, the holy and precious food, the food of ru'ach and neshamah, is the food of the distant, supernal, precious-above-all place, being the food of the colleagues who strive in Torah, and it is the food that comes from the supernal Chokhmah. And why is this place different? Because Torah emerges from the supernal Chokhmah, and those who strive in Torah enter into the essence of the root, and therefore their food comes from that supernal, holy place. Rabbi Elazar came and kissed his hands and said, happy is my portion that I stand at these words - happy is the portion of the righteous who strive in Torah day and night, for it merits them in this world and in the World to Come, as it is written (Deuteronomy 30:20), "for it is your life and the length of your days" - to this point. And the intent is "your life" in this world, and "length of days" in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:74: And so, there were several Torah scholars who were wealthy, like Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom (Yoma 35b) - and if so, would the wealthy Torah scholar have lost out, that his food not be flowed from above? And so Rabbi Pinchas appears to have been wealthy, as is proven in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, end of page 59). And we also find Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, peace be upon him, of whom they said, in the chapter "HaSocher et HaPo'alim" (Bava Metzia 84b), that he would eat sixty kinds of food when he was ill. Rather, certainly the flow bestowed in the food when a person eats shall be coarse and thick, or fine - for the rest of the people, a coarse and thick flow is bestowed, which is the sustenance of the body; and for Torah scholars, a fine flow is bestowed from above, for the sustenance of the soul, as explained - and this is (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - meaning that the righteous person, in his eating, does not intend the health of his body and that it be strong, but rather "to satisfy his soul," in order to give sustenance to his soul, so that the supernal flow be bestowed in that food, and through this his soul is satisfied. And certainly, through the prayer they would pray for their food, as we copied above, that Rabbi Yesa would say, "now is the time it is given from the King's house" - the flow of the soul would be fine and spiritual - and this is "from the King's house," which is the Shechinah, who has already received the supernal flow, the food of Torah scholars, to bestow it upon them, unlike the rest of the people. And likewise through the intent of eating, as explained above.
